The project built a SOM from scratch, made it a DTW-SOM, and tested fourteen
variants on twelve data sets, plus chaos, rings and tearing maps. The growing
DTW-SOM was the best of its family and DTW the biggest single lever; chaos
and tearing lost to the plain controls that do the same job. This page asks
**what to build next** for two uses: **detecting and classifying partial
discharges** from their waveforms, and **classifying movements** from sensor
series. It has three parts:

1. **The ideas** (Sections 1 to 3): what the benchmarks already decided, a
   catalogue of improvements gathered from seven angles (distances, physics,
   the structure of the map, partial-discharge engineering, movement
   recognition, numerical precision, and evaluation), each with the plain
   control it must beat seed by seed, and a bridge from physics to the code.
2. **A demonstrator** (Sections 4 to 7): the online SOM rewritten once, with
   nine distances in the winner choice *and* in the update, six training
   ingredients that each test one idea, four map sizes, all the project's
   measures plus trustworthiness, continuity and detection AUROC, on three
   data sets (a CBF, a synthetic stand-in for the partial discharges, and
   three-axis gestures), 2 seeds each, every variant judged against
   its family's control with the same start and order of items.
3. **The precision ladder** (Section 8): the same map in fp32, fp64, 80-bit,
   128-bit and 256-bit MPFR arithmetic, step by step.

<div class="box">
**The answer in short** (2 seeds, 2 passes, 7 &times; 7 maps unless said otherwise; the synthetic stand-ins of Section 2)

* **The distance is the lever, and it must sit in the update.** On the
  partial-discharge stand-in the classes were found best by the
  DTW-SOM (ARI 0.34 against 0.18
  for the online SOM and 0.34 for the DTW-SOM); on the gestures by
  the DTW-SOM (0.50 against 0.43).
  Manhattan, Chebyshev, cosine, correlation and the shape-based distance each
  change the winner for a reason, and the update stays a straight line
  towards the item; only DTW, soft-DTW and SBD change what the item looks
  like to the prototype.
* **Detection is a different question from classification.** With a map
  trained on noise alone and the distance to the winner as the alarm, the
  Correlation (1 - r) told discharges from noise best (AUROC
  0.88, online SOM 0.64): a quiet
  corona pulse is *closer* to the noise map than noise itself in the
  Euclidean distance, so an amplitude-blind distance is what detection
  needs.
* **Physics gives two exact temperatures and several metaphors.** Soft-DTW is
  the free energy of all alignments at a temperature gamma, and its gradient
  is the expected alignment that the update uses; deterministic annealing
  puts a temperature on the winner. Both are principled where the chaotic
  clocks were not. On these data soft-DTW beat the DTW-SOM on fit (QE judged
  with DTW) on 0 of 2, 0 of 2, 1 of 2
  seeds (CBF, PD, gestures), and the annealed winner changed the order of
  the Euclidean map (TE better on 0 of 2, 1 of 2, 0 of 2
  seeds) more than its fit (QE better on 0 of 2, 0 of 2, 0 of 2).
* **The map size changes who wins.** Read the charts of Section 6 at four
  sizes before choosing: the best distance for the classes on the
  partial-discharge stand-in was DTW-SOM
  from 5 &times; 5 to 14 &times; 14, and every fit measure falls with the number of
  units whatever the map does (the project's trap, Section 4 of the metrics page).
* **Precision: fp64 is the right stop.** With the same seed, fp64, 80-bit,
  128-bit and 256-bit MPFR chose the same winner at every one of
  the 360 steps on the small CBF
  (0
  flips, prototypes within 6\times 10^{-15});
  fp32 first chose a different winner at step NA
  and then went its own way. A near-tie closer than fp32's resolution happened in
  0% of the steps, closer than fp64's in
  0%. MPFR is a reference oracle
  (0.5 s in C for what fp64 does in
  0.00 s), not a training tool; the precision
  question that matters for a field detector is the other way round, fp32 or
  fixed point on a microcontroller, with fp64 as the oracle.
* **What to build first** (Section 9): the distance study on the real PD
  waveforms and real gestures, the amplitude-blind novelty detector, soft-DTW
  and the annealed winner ported into the growing DTW-SOM, and a GNG-style
  edge rule as the principled form of tear-and-rejoin. Not first: chaos,
  tearing by link length, MPFR training, momentum.
</div>

# 1. What the benchmarks already decided

Seven reports tested every change one at a time, seed by seed, against the
plain map that does the same job. These are the findings that bind any new
idea, with the report they come from:


```r
lessons <- data.frame(
  Lesson = c("DTW belongs in the update, not only in the winner choice",
             "DTW or not depends on the data more than any variant does",
             "The window is a property of the data",
             "Fit and order pull against each other; growing maps won on both",
             "Chaos never beat the plain rival that does the same job",
             "Tearing never beat a smaller start radius",
             "Part of DTW's gain is in reading the map, not in training it",
             "No single score decides; compare only same size, same data, same distance",
             "Prototypes lose their timing under DTW; births from the data give it back"),
  Evidence = c("DTW for the winner only gave the worst fit of all (QE higher than the DTW-SOM on all series sets).",
               "ARI better by more than 0.1 on CBF and Synthetic Control, worse by more than 0.1 on the solar I-V curves, where the position of a feature is the information.",
               "CBF: ARI 0.24 at a 10% window, 0.92 at 20%; solar I-V curves better at 5%.",
               "Batch: best QE, worse TE and KL; CHAOSOM: the opposite; growing SOM and growing DTW-SOM: lower QE, TE and KL on most sets.",
               "Restarts at even steps did what CHAOSOM's spikes did; the smooth long-run output did what the chaotic units did; chaotic units hurt everywhere (their memory, not the chaos).",
               "On 18 data sets and 3 sizes, tearing was never better than all three radius maps on QE and TE together; rejoining or mending did not rescue it.",
               "On the partial discharges the online SOM mapped and clustered with DTW came close to the DTW-SOM's ARI.",
               "QE, EV and KL fall with more units; TE is near 0 on tiny maps; purity rises with units; DTW is never above the Euclidean distance.",
               "Timing error 3.6 to 2.0 time points on CBF; the floating neighbourhood gives back the order the births cost."),
  Where = c("Tutorial 11a; benchmark", "Benchmark 10", "Benchmark 8", "Benchmark 7, 10", "Tutorial 13; chaotic units", "Tearing lab; tear and join",
            "Benchmark 10", "Metrics; benchmark 4", "Tutorial 12"),
  `What it means here` = c("Every new distance in Section 4 comes with its own update step.",
                           "The demonstrator runs every distance on three kinds of data and reads them separately.",
                           "The band is 10% of the length everywhere here, as in the benchmark; the window study is tier A of the roadmap.",
                           "The annealed winner and the lattice variants are read on TE and KL next to QE.",
                           "Every ingredient below has a mechanism and a control; the two temperatures (Sections 3 and 4) are the principled replacements.",
                           "Tear-and-rejoin returns as a rule by data support (GNG edges), not by link length.",
                           "Every map is judged with the Euclidean distance, with DTW and with its own; detection uses the own distance.",
                           "Every chart has a map-size axis; the strips compare a variant with its control at the same size and seed.",
                           "The growing DTW-SOM is the vehicle for the winners of this page; it is not rebuilt here."),
  check.names = FALSE)
tab(lessons, search = FALSE)
```

# 2. The two targets and the data of this page

**Partial discharges.** The project's PD set is airborne ultrasound of
corona, air-gap and void discharges plus ambient noise, 125 samples at
500 kS/s triggered by the current pulse, loudness over four orders of
magnitude, pressure used as asinh(p / 1 mPa). A PD engineer reads three
things from such a pulse: its *shape* (rise, ringing frequency, decay, a
reflection), its *loudness*, and, when a mains-phase reference exists, its
*phase* (the PRPD pattern). The map must therefore (a) use a distance that
reads shape without being ruled by loudness, (b) keep loudness somewhere it
can be read, as a channel or a per-unit statistic, and (c) answer two
questions: *is this a discharge?* (detection, with a false-alarm rate on
noise) and *which kind?* (classification).

**Movement.** A gesture or an activity comes from several axes at once, at
its own speed, held in a sensor that is never oriented the same way twice.
The map must align in time (DTW, soft-DTW, or a rigid shift), treat the axes
together (one alignment for all channels), and be read against the 1-NN DTW
baseline that any template matcher reaches.

**This knit uses synthetic stand-ins**, because the project's data (som_bench/data/datasets.rds) is not in this checkout; put it there and the loader uses the real CBF, the real partial discharges and GunPoint instead (Section 4 shows the loader).
Each stand-in is built to have the difficulty that matters for its target:

<p class="note">1-NN accuracy: leave-one-out nearest-neighbour classification, the floor for any
map that is then read with the same distance. The gap between the Euclidean and the DTW column says
how much a time alignment can buy on each set.</p>

## A few items of every class {.tabset .tabset-pills}


```r
example_plot <- function(d, per_class = 4) {
  col <- class_colours(d$cls)
  show <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_along(d$cls), d$cls), function(i) head(i, per_class)))
  pl <- plot_ly()
  for (ch in seq_len(d$nch)) for (i in show) {
    y <- d$X[i, (ch - 1) * d$L + seq_len(d$L)]
    pl <- add_trace(pl, x = seq_len(d$L), y = y, type = "scatter", mode = "lines", xaxis = paste0("x", ch), yaxis = paste0("y", ch),
                    line = list(color = adjustcolor(col[[as.character(d$cls[i])]], 0.75), width = 1.3),
                    name = as.character(d$cls[i]), legendgroup = as.character(d$cls[i]), showlegend = ch == 1 && i == show[match(d$cls[i], d$cls[show])],
                    hovertemplate = paste0(as.character(d$cls[i]), ", item ", i, if (d$nch > 1) paste0(", axis ", ch), "<br>t = %{x}: %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"))
  }
  lay <- list(margin = list(t = 20, b = 40), legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.15), showlegend = TRUE)
  for (ch in seq_len(d$nch)) {
    dom <- c((ch - 1) / d$nch + 0.02 * (ch > 1), ch / d$nch - 0.02 * (ch < d$nch))
    lay[[paste0("xaxis", if (ch > 1) ch else "")]] <- ax(if (ch == d$nch) d$x_label else NULL, domain = dom, anchor = paste0("y", ch))
    lay[[paste0("yaxis", if (ch > 1) ch else "")]] <- ax(if (d$nch > 1) paste("axis", ch) else NULL, anchor = paste0("x", ch))
  }
  do.call(chart, c(list(pl), lay))
}
for (k in names(datasets)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", SHORT[[k]], "\n\n", sep = "")
  print(tagList(example_plot(datasets[[k]])))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

# 3. The ideas

The brainstorm was run from seven angles, each idea then handed to a skeptic
from another angle who tried to refute it: is it already tested in the
project, is the mechanism real or a knob without a reason, are the
references right, is the control fair, does it plausibly matter for pulses
or for gestures. What survived is below; what was dropped is listed at the
end of the section with the reason. Tier A: build first; B: after A pays
off; C: a long shot worth one small experiment. Filter with the menus above
the table; the folded cells open on a click.


```r
if (is.null(ideas)) {
  cat("The catalogue (next_steps/ideas/ideas.json) is not in this checkout.")
} else {
  fold <- function(s, n = 90) ifelse(nchar(s) > n, sprintf("<details><summary>%s&hellip;</summary>%s</details>", substr(s, 1, n), s), s)
  it <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ideas$ideas, function(i) data.frame(
    Tier = i$tier, Lens = i$lens, Idea = sprintf("<b>%s</b>", i$title),
    `What it changes` = fold(paste(i$what_it_changes, i$mechanism)), `For partial discharges` = fold(i$why_pd),
    `For movement` = fold(i$why_movement), `The control to beat` = fold(i$control), `How to test` = fold(i$how_to_test),
    Cost = fold(i$cost, 60), `Expected gain` = i$expected_gain, Confidence = sprintf("%.2f", i$confidence),
    `Skeptic` = fold(paste(if (nzchar(i$problems)) i$problems else "no objection", if (nzchar(i$corrections)) paste("Correction:", i$corrections) else ""), 70),
    References = fold(paste(unlist(i$anchors), collapse = "; "), 60), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, check.names = FALSE)))
  it <- it[order(match(it$Tier, c("A", "B", "C")), -as.numeric(it$Confidence)), ]
  chip_js <- JS("function(data, type) { if (type !== 'display') return data; return '<span class=\"chip ' + data + '\">' + data + '</span>'; }")
  filtered_table(it, c("Tier", "Lens"), id = "ideas-table", escape = FALSE, dom = "ti", page_length = 100,
                 column_defs = list(list(render = chip_js, targets = 0), list(width = "12%", targets = 2), list(width = "16%", targets = 3)),
                 ordering = TRUE, paging = FALSE)
}
```

## 3a. Distances: what each one reads, and what its update does

A SOM has two places for a distance: the **contest** (which unit wins) and
the **update** (how the item pulls the prototype). The project learned the
hard way that the two must agree. For the pointwise distances the update
needs no change: the straight line from a prototype to an item is a
geodesic of every norm, so "move a share of the way towards the item" is
the right step for L1, L2, Chebyshev and Minkowski alike; what changes is
*which* prototype moves, and that is what matters.

* **Manhattan (L1)**: the winner is the prototype with the smallest *sum of
  absolute* differences. One loud sample (a spike, a glitch) counts in
  proportion to its size, not its square, so L1 is the first thing to try
  when outliers rule the Euclidean contest. Its natural partner is the
  **clipped pull** (the Huber step of Section 4): the pull of every sample is
  capped, so one loud item cannot drag a prototype.
* **Chebyshev (L-infinity)**: only the worst sample counts. It is the
  distance of a tolerance band and is sharp on sets where one feature decides
  (a step that is or is not there), blunt where everything is noisy.
* **Minkowski p**: between the two; p = 3 is the Euclidean contest with
  large differences weighed more.
* **Cosine and correlation**: the angle between item and prototype, with or
  without their means removed. Loudness drops out entirely. For partial
  discharges that is exactly the question *is it the same shape?* asked
  without *how loud?*, which is why Section 7 finds them where it does.
  Loudness then has to be kept elsewhere: as a per-unit statistic, or as an
  extra channel (the easiest test: append asinh(peak) as a 126th value with a
  weight).
* **Shape-based distance (SBD, from k-Shape)**: one global shift instead of
  a warp, found by cross-correlation; the update shifts the item by the best
  lag. It is the rigid cousin of DTW: it reads a pulse that came 3 samples
  late as the same pulse, costs L times less than DTW, and cannot stretch
  the inside of a series. For trigger-aligned pulses with a jitter it is the
  first thing to try before DTW.
* **DTW** (the project's) and **soft-DTW**: Section 3c.
* **Not built here, worth building**: dependent *vs* independent
  multivariate DTW for the gestures (one path for all axes against one path
  per axis), MSM and TWED (elastic measures with a cost for every edit, the
  strongest in the UCR bake-offs), the lower bounds that make DTW cheap at
  mapping time (the project has LB_Keogh), and distances on transformed
  series (the log-spectrum or the envelope of a pulse, where the ringing
  frequency and the decay become positions).

## 3b. The map: growing, tearing, rejoining, done by data support

The project's growing DTW-SOM won on fit, order and timing; its tearing map
lost to a smaller start radius because a link broken by *length* is the
same knob as a weaker pull, applied unevenly. The structural ideas that
survived the skeptics share one principle: **let the data, not a threshold on
length, decide what is connected.**

* **Growing neural gas (Fritzke 1995) edges on the SOM lattice.** An edge
  between two units is born when they are the winner and runner-up of an
  item, and it ages every step it is not; old edges die. This is tear-and-
  rejoin as the user wants it, with a reason for every tear and every
  rejoin: an edge is kept exactly as long as items keep landing on both ends.
  The control: the growing DTW-SOM with its fixed lattice; the test: QE, TE,
  KL and the number of pieces on the three-blob data where tearing helped
  and on the 18 sets where it did not.
* **Pruning idle units and a stop rule** (the project lists both as
  untested): remove a unit that wins nothing for a full pass; stop growing
  when a new unit no longer lowers the Kaski-Lagus error on held-out seeds.
* **A torus** for cyclic data: when the PD data carry the mains phase, the
  map's one axis should be a circle. Section 6 tests the plain torus against
  the rectangular sheet (its control); on data with no cycle it should not
  help, and the rim effects it removes should show in TE.
* **Conscience** (DeSieno 1988): a unit that wins too often is handicapped.
  It targets dead units and unequal classes (quiet corona against loud
  air-gap discharges); a neighbourhood already prevents most dead units, so
  the expected gain is small and the test is cheap.
* **LVQ fine-tuning** when labels exist: Kohonen's LVQ1 after the
  unsupervised map, moving prototypes a little towards their own class and
  away from others; the control is the unsupervised map read by Ward
  clustering, the measure purity and ARI on held-out items.

## 3c. Physics: two temperatures, one tension, and the metaphors


```r
if (!is.null(ideas) && nzchar(ideas$physics_bridge)) cat(ideas$physics_bridge, "\n\n")
```

The parts of that bridge that the demonstrator tests, in the words of the
code:

* <span class="chip exact">exact</span> **Soft-DTW is a free energy.** DTW
  takes the cheapest alignment; soft-DTW takes
  &minus;&gamma;&nbsp;log&nbsp;&Sigma;<sub>paths</sub>&nbsp;exp(&minus;cost/&gamma;),
  the free energy of all alignments at temperature &gamma; (Cuturi &
  Blondel 2017). Its gradient with respect to the prototype is the
  Boltzmann-weighted average of the alignments, the matrix E of the core,
  and the update of Section 4 averages the item with exactly those weights:
  the soft barycentre step. As &gamma; &rarr; 0 the path, the distance and the
  update all become DTW's (the check in Section 4 shows the two agree to
  10<sup>&minus;12</sup> at &gamma; = 0.001). One number, &gamma;, replaces the
  hard choice of one path with a smooth one; it costs about ten times DTW.
* <span class="chip exact">exact</span> **Deterministic annealing is a
  temperature on the winner.** Write the SOM's cost of assigning item x to
  unit k as E<sub>k</sub> = &Sigma;<sub>j</sub> h<sub>kj</sub> d(x, m<sub>j</sub>)<sup>2</sup>
  and let the item pull every unit with the Boltzmann weight
  P(k) &prop; exp(&minus;E<sub>k</sub>/T) (Graepel, Burger & Obermayer 1997;
  Heskes 1999 for why this is the winner that makes the SOM a gradient
  descent). At T &rarr; 0 the most probable unit takes all and the loop is
  Kohonen's; at high T every unit pulls alike and the map sits at the mean
  of the data, exactly the contracted state of the chaotic page's trap; as T
  falls the map unfolds, in order, through the phase transitions that split
  it along the principal axes of the data (Rose 1998). The radius schedule
  already plays part of this role, which is why the experiment, not the
  argument, decides whether annealing on top of a radius schedule buys
  anything: Section 6.
* <span class="chip exact">exact</span> **Magnification.** A 1-D SOM places
  prototypes with density p(x)<sup>2/3</sup> (Ritter & Schulten 1986), not
  p(x): it under-represents dense regions and over-represents sparse ones.
  Conscience pushes the exponent towards 1 (equal use of all units);
  Bauer, Der & Herrmann (1996) give a local learning rate that sets any
  exponent, including the information-optimal one for detection, where rare
  (sparse) pulses deserve more units, not fewer.
* <span class="chip metaphor">metaphor</span> **Springs and fracture.** The
  lattice as springs between prototypes with the neighbourhood as the
  stiffness, and a link that tears when its strain energy exceeds a Griffith
  threshold. Honest reading: the stiffness *is* the radius, and a tear by
  stored energy is a tear by length squared, the project's rule with another
  exponent. The elastic net of Durbin & Willshaw (1987) is the exact version
  of this energy for the ring; for a sheet the useful part of the idea is
  healing by data support, which is the GNG rule of Section 3b.
* <span class="chip metaphor">metaphor</span> **Inertia (momentum).** A
  prototype that keeps a velocity. Cheap to test (Section 6), no mechanism
  that says it should help an online map with a decaying rate, and a known
  way to overshoot small clusters.
* <span class="chip metaphor">metaphor</span> **Replica exchange.** Several
  maps at different temperatures that swap; for a SOM this is *restarts with
  the best map kept*, which the ring experiments already found to be the
  working part of CHAOSOM. The principled version keeps the map with the
  lowest energy in Heskes' sense, not the shortest tour.

## 3d. Precision and the opposite direction

The user asked about fp64 data and an MPFR-precise map. Section 8 answers
with measurements; the reasoning is short. A SOM's state is the prototypes;
the only place a tiny numerical difference can grow is a **contest decided
by a near-tie**: if two prototypes are within the arithmetic's resolution of
each other, the winner can flip, and from that step on the two runs diverge
(the chaotic page saw the same with nudges of 10<sup>-3</sup>, and nothing
below 10<sup>-6</sup>). So the question is how often a contest is that
close, which the core now records at every step (the relative gap between
the first and the second distance). DTW adds a second place: the min over
three cells of a DP table, where a tie picks a path, but the cost is the
same whichever path is taken, and the warp differs only at ties that the
update then averages. The other direction is the one that matters for a
detector in the field: a map stored and evaluated in fp32, fp16 or
fixed-point integers on a microcontroller, with fp64 as the oracle. The
ladder of Section 8 is that oracle test run upwards.

## 3e. Measuring across map sizes and for detection

* **Fair across sizes**: EV (a share, not a distance), the share of units
  used, purity against its random-units line, ARI and NMI (chance-corrected),
  and ranks within a size. Every fit measure that is a distance (QE, KL)
  falls with units; read it only within one size.
* **Trustworthiness and continuity** (Venna & Kaski 2001): are an item's k
  nearest items in the data its neighbours on the map (trust), and are its
  map neighbours its data neighbours (continuity)? Unlike TE they read the
  whole neighbourhood, not the runner-up alone, and unlike TP they do not
  react to the outline of the map. Computed here on the units' map
  distances against the Euclidean neighbourhoods of the items.
* **Detection**: train on the background, score every item by its distance
  to the winner, read the ROC. AUROC overall and per class: the per-class
  numbers show which discharges the map would miss.
* **Wins seed by seed** are counts, not p-values; with
  2 seeds, "better on all seeds" is the only strong statement, and
  a difference inside the seed-to-seed spread is noise whatever its sign.


```r
if (!is.null(ideas) && length(ideas$dropped)) {
  cat("<details><summary>Ideas the skeptics dropped, and why</summary>\n\n")
  dr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ideas$dropped, function(d) data.frame(Idea = d$title, Lens = d$lens, `Why it was dropped` = d$why_dropped, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))
  print(tab(dr, search = TRUE))
  cat("\n\n</details>\n\n")
}
if (!is.null(ideas) && length(ideas$gaps)) {
  cat("<details><summary>What the completeness critic still found missing</summary>\n\n")
  for (g in ideas$gaps) cat(sprintf("* **%s.** %s *Fix:* %s\n", g$title, g$why_it_matters, g$suggested_fix))
  cat("\n\n</details>\n\n")
}
```

# 4. The demonstrator

One online SOM, written once in C++ as a template over the scalar type, with
the distance as an argument of both the contest and the update, and five
ingredients that each switch one idea on. It is not the project's core and
does not try to match it to the last bit; it follows the same conventions
(hexagonal lattice, Gaussian neighbourhood, learning rate 0.5 &rarr; 0.01,
kohonen's start radius &rarr; 0 used as 0.5 below 1, the start and the
order of items drawn from the seed), so that a variant and its control see
the same items in the same order from the same start.


```r
vt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(VARIANTS, function(v) data.frame(
  Variant = v$label, Group = v$group, Distance = v$mode, Lattice = paste(v$topo, if (v$torus) "torus" else "sheet"),
  Control = VARIANTS[[v$family]]$label, `What it changes` = v$what, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)))
vt$Control[vt$Variant == vt$Control] <- ""
tab(vt, search = FALSE)
```

Settings that come from the data so that one value means the same thing
everywhere: the DTW band and the SBD shift are 10% of the length; soft-DTW's
&gamma; is 0.1 of the variance of one sample; the clipped pull caps each
component at one standard deviation of a sample; the annealing temperature
starts at the mean squared distance of the items to their mean (under the
map's own distance) and falls geometrically by a factor 1000 over the first
90% of the steps, then the winner is hard; conscience uses &beta; = 0.25 and
a win-share memory of 10<sup>4</sup> steps; momentum keeps half of the last
step.

**Checks.** The core's DTW equals a plain R implementation (squared local
cost, Sakoe-Chiba band) on 200 random pairs; soft-DTW converges to DTW
squared as &gamma; &rarr; 0 and its expected-alignment warp to DTW's path
average (10<sup>-12</sup> at &gamma; = 0.001); the pointwise distances equal
R's `dist()`; dependent multichannel DTW scales as it should; the online SOM
in fp64 equals the same loop written in R to the last bit; the topographic
product is 0 on an ordered chain and negative on a scrambled one; the
Kaski-Lagus way along an ordered chain is the sum of its links. The script
is `next_steps/tests/test_core.R`.

The code, in full:


```cpp
// ns_core.cpp: the compiled core of som_next_steps.Rmd
//
// One online SOM, written once as a template over the scalar type, so that the same loop can run in
// fp32 (float), fp64 (double), 80-bit extended (long double) and 128-bit quad (__float128); the
// 256-bit reference runs in R with Rmpfr (next_steps/R/ns_precision.R) and repeats these operations.
//
// Every row of X is one item: a series of L points in nch channels, stored channel by channel
// (value at time i of channel c is x[c * L + i]); a feature vector is a series with nch = 1.
//
// Distances (the 'mode' argument), each with the step that moves a prototype towards an item:
//   0 EUCLID      sqrt(sum (x - m)^2)                 m += a h (x - m)
//   1 MANHATTAN   sum |x - m|                         same step (a straight line is a geodesic of L1 too)
//   2 CHEBYSHEV   max |x - m|                         same step
//   3 MINKOWSKI   (sum |x - m|^p)^(1/p)               same step
//   4 COSINE      1 - <x, m> / (|x| |m|)              same step
//   5 CORRELATION 1 - Pearson(x, m)                   same step
//   6 DTW         sqrt(DTW cost, Sakoe-Chiba band)    x is warped onto m's time axis along the path first
//   7 SOFTDTW     soft-DTW value (Cuturi & Blondel)   x is warped by the expected alignment E (soft barycentre step)
//   8 SBD         1 - max normalised cross-correlation  x is shifted by the best lag first (k-Shape)
// Multichannel series use the dependent form of DTW, soft-DTW and SBD: one alignment for all channels.
//
// Options of the training loop (all off = the online SOM of the project, Gaussian neighbourhood):
//   temp[s] > 0   soft winner (deterministic annealing, Graepel, Burger & Obermayer): P(k | x) is a
//                 softmax of -(sum_j h_kj d_j^2) / temp over the units, and unit j moves with weight
//                 sum_k P(k) h_kj instead of h_{win, j}
//   conscience    frequency-sensitive winner (Ahalt et al. 1990 / DeSieno 1988): the winner minimises
//                 d_k (1 + beta (K p_k - 1)), with p_k the running share of wins of unit k
//   huber > 0     every component of the pull x - m is clipped to [-huber, huber] (a robust, L1-like step)
//   momentum > 0  heavy-ball update: v = mu v + a h (x - m); m += v
//   kahan         Neumaier-compensated sums in the pointwise distances (fp64 and below)
//
// [[Rcpp::plugins(cpp17)]]
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include <quadmath.h>
#include <cmath>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <limits>
using namespace Rcpp;

enum { EUCLID = 0, MANHATTAN = 1, CHEBYSHEV = 2, MINKOWSKI = 3, COSINE = 4, CORRELATION = 5,
       DTW = 6, SOFTDTW = 7, SBD = 8 };
enum { P_FLOAT = 0, P_DOUBLE = 1, P_LONGDOUBLE = 2, P_QUAD = 3 };

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- scalar helpers
template <typename T> inline T t_sqrt(T x) { return std::sqrt(x); }
template <typename T> inline T t_exp(T x)  { return std::exp(x); }
template <typename T> inline T t_log(T x)  { return std::log(x); }
template <typename T> inline T t_abs(T x)  { return std::fabs(x); }
template <typename T> inline T t_pow(T x, T y) { return std::pow(x, y); }
template <> inline __float128 t_sqrt(__float128 x) { return sqrtq(x); }
template <> inline __float128 t_exp(__float128 x)  { return expq(x); }
template <> inline __float128 t_log(__float128 x)  { return logq(x); }
template <> inline __float128 t_abs(__float128 x)  { return fabsq(x); }
template <> inline __float128 t_pow(__float128 x, __float128 y) { return powq(x, y); }

template <typename T> inline T big() { return T(1e300); }   // 'infinity' inside the DP tables

struct Opts {
  int mode, L, nch, band, maxshift;
  double p, gamma;
  bool kahan;
};

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- pointwise distances
template <typename T>
struct Sum {                                      // plain or Neumaier-compensated running sum
  T s = 0, c = 0; bool kahan;
  explicit Sum(bool k) : kahan(k) {}
  inline void add(T v) {
    if (!kahan) { s += v; return; }
    T t = s + v;
    if (t_abs(s) >= t_abs(v)) c += (s - t) + v; else c += (v - t) + s;
    s = t;
  }
  inline T value() const { return kahan ? s + c : s; }
};

template <typename T>
T pointwise(const T* x, const T* m, int D, const Opts& o) {
  switch (o.mode) {
    case EUCLID: { Sum<T> s(o.kahan); for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) { T d = x[i] - m[i]; s.add(d * d); } return t_sqrt(s.value()); }
    case MANHATTAN: { Sum<T> s(o.kahan); for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) s.add(t_abs(x[i] - m[i])); return s.value(); }
    case CHEBYSHEV: { T mx = 0; for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) { T d = t_abs(x[i] - m[i]); if (d > mx) mx = d; } return mx; }
    case MINKOWSKI: { Sum<T> s(o.kahan); T p = T(o.p); for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) s.add(t_pow(t_abs(x[i] - m[i]), p));
                      return t_pow(s.value(), T(1) / p); }
    case COSINE: { Sum<T> xy(o.kahan), xx(o.kahan), mm(o.kahan);
                   for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) { xy.add(x[i] * m[i]); xx.add(x[i] * x[i]); mm.add(m[i] * m[i]); }
                   T den = t_sqrt(xx.value()) * t_sqrt(mm.value());
                   return den > 0 ? T(1) - xy.value() / den : T(1); }
    case CORRELATION: { T mx = 0, mm_ = 0; for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) { mx += x[i]; mm_ += m[i]; } mx /= D; mm_ /= D;
                        Sum<T> xy(o.kahan), xx(o.kahan), mm(o.kahan);
                        for (int i = 0; i < D; i++) { T a = x[i] - mx, b = m[i] - mm_; xy.add(a * b); xx.add(a * a); mm.add(b * b); }
                        T den = t_sqrt(xx.value()) * t_sqrt(mm.value());
                        return den > 0 ? T(1) - xy.value() / den : T(1); }
  }
  return 0;
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- DTW
// local cost between time i of x and time j of m: the squared distance over the channels
template <typename T>
inline T local_cost(const T* x, const T* m, int i, int j, int L, int nch) {
  T c = 0;
  for (int ch = 0; ch < nch; ch++) { T d = x[ch * L + i] - m[ch * L + j]; c += d * d; }
  return c;
}

// the DP table of DTW: (L + 1) x (L + 1), row 0 and column 0 are the border; returns sqrt(cost)
template <typename T>
T dtw_table(const T* x, const T* m, const Opts& o, std::vector<T>& R) {
  const int L = o.L, W = L + 1, b = o.band;
  R.assign((size_t) W * W, big<T>());
  R[0] = 0;
  for (int i = 1; i <= L; i++) {
    int lo = std::max(1, i - b), hi = std::min(L, i + b);
    for (int j = lo; j <= hi; j++) {
      T best = R[(size_t) (i - 1) * W + (j - 1)];
      T up = R[(size_t) (i - 1) * W + j], left = R[(size_t) i * W + (j - 1)];
      if (up < best) best = up;
      if (left < best) best = left;
      R[(size_t) i * W + j] = local_cost(x, m, i - 1, j - 1, L, o.nch) + best;
    }
  }
  return t_sqrt(R[(size_t) L * W + L]);
}

// walk the path back and average, for every prototype point j, the item points matched with it
template <typename T>
void dtw_warp(const T* x, const Opts& o, const std::vector<T>& R, T* xw) {
  const int L = o.L, W = L + 1;
  std::vector<int> cnt(L, 0);
  for (int k = 0; k < L * o.nch; k++) xw[k] = 0;
  int i = L, j = L;
  while (i > 0 && j > 0) {
    for (int ch = 0; ch < o.nch; ch++) xw[ch * L + (j - 1)] += x[ch * L + (i - 1)];
    cnt[j - 1]++;
    if (i == 1 && j == 1) break;
    T d = R[(size_t) (i - 1) * W + (j - 1)], u = R[(size_t) (i - 1) * W + j], l = R[(size_t) i * W + (j - 1)];
    if (d <= u && d <= l) { i--; j--; }            // ties: the diagonal first, then the item's time, then the prototype's
    else if (u <= l) i--;
    else j--;
  }
  for (int j2 = 0; j2 < L; j2++) if (cnt[j2] > 0) for (int ch = 0; ch < o.nch; ch++) xw[ch * L + j2] /= T(cnt[j2]);
}

// ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ soft-DTW
template <typename T>
inline T softmin3(T a, T b, T c, T g) {
  T m = a; if (b < m) m = b; if (c < m) m = c;
  if (m >= big<T>() / 2) return big<T>();
  T s = t_exp(-(a - m) / g) + t_exp(-(b - m) / g) + t_exp(-(c - m) / g);
  return m - g * t_log(s);
}

// forward pass; R is (L + 2) x (L + 2) so that the backward pass has its padding row and column
template <typename T>
T softdtw_table(const T* x, const T* m, const Opts& o, std::vector<T>& R) {
  const int L = o.L, W = L + 2, b = o.band;
  const T g = T(o.gamma);
  R.assign((size_t) W * W, big<T>());
  R[0] = 0;
  for (int i = 1; i <= L; i++) {
    int lo = std::max(1, i - b), hi = std::min(L, i + b);
    for (int j = lo; j <= hi; j++)
      R[(size_t) i * W + j] = local_cost(x, m, i - 1, j - 1, L, o.nch)
        + softmin3(R[(size_t) (i - 1) * W + (j - 1)], R[(size_t) (i - 1) * W + j], R[(size_t) i * W + (j - 1)], g);
  }
  return R[(size_t) L * W + L];
}

// backward pass: E[i, j] is the expected number of times (i, j) lies on the alignment under the Gibbs
// distribution over paths at temperature gamma; xw[j] = sum_i E[i, j] x[i] / sum_i E[i, j]
template <typename T>
void softdtw_warp(const T* x, const T* m, const Opts& o, std::vector<T>& R, T* xw) {
  const int L = o.L, W = L + 2, b = o.band;
  const T g = T(o.gamma), BIG = big<T>();
  std::vector<T> E((size_t) W * W, T(0)), delta((size_t) W * W, T(0));
  for (int i = 1; i <= L; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= L; j++)
    if (std::abs(i - j) <= b) delta[(size_t) i * W + j] = local_cost(x, m, i - 1, j - 1, L, o.nch);
  // padding as in Cuturi & Blondel (2017), Algorithm 2
  for (int k = 0; k <= L + 1; k++) { R[(size_t) k * W + (L + 1)] = -BIG; R[(size_t) (L + 1) * W + k] = -BIG; }
  R[(size_t) (L + 1) * W + (L + 1)] = R[(size_t) L * W + L];
  E[(size_t) (L + 1) * W + (L + 1)] = 1;
  for (int j = L; j >= 1; j--) {
    for (int i = L; i >= 1; i--) {
      T r = R[(size_t) i * W + j];
      if (r >= BIG / 2 || std::abs(i - j) > b) continue;          // outside the band: no path passes here
      T a = 0, bb = 0, c = 0;
      T r1 = R[(size_t) (i + 1) * W + j], r2 = R[(size_t) i * W + (j + 1)], r3 = R[(size_t) (i + 1) * W + (j + 1)];
      if (r1 < BIG / 2 && r1 > -BIG / 2) a  = t_exp((r1 - r - delta[(size_t) (i + 1) * W + j]) / g);
      if (r2 < BIG / 2 && r2 > -BIG / 2) bb = t_exp((r2 - r - delta[(size_t) i * W + (j + 1)]) / g);
      if (r3 < BIG / 2 && r3 > -BIG / 2) c  = t_exp((r3 - r - delta[(size_t) (i + 1) * W + (j + 1)]) / g);
      E[(size_t) i * W + j] = a * E[(size_t) (i + 1) * W + j] + bb * E[(size_t) i * W + (j + 1)] + c * E[(size_t) (i + 1) * W + (j + 1)];
    }
  }
  for (int k = 0; k < L * o.nch; k++) xw[k] = 0;
  for (int j = 1; j <= L; j++) {
    T tot = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= L; i++) {
      T e = E[(size_t) i * W + j];
      if (e <= 0) continue;
      tot += e;
      for (int ch = 0; ch < o.nch; ch++) xw[ch * L + (j - 1)] += e * x[ch * L + (i - 1)];
    }
    if (tot > 0) for (int ch = 0; ch < o.nch; ch++) xw[ch * L + (j - 1)] /= tot;
    else for (int ch = 0; ch < o.nch; ch++) xw[ch * L + (j - 1)] = m[ch * L + (j - 1)];   // cannot happen inside the band
  }
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- SBD
// cross-correlation over lags -maxshift..maxshift, summed over the channels; returns 1 - max NCC and the lag
template <typename T>
T sbd_dist(const T* x, const T* m, const Opts& o, int* best_lag) {
  const int L = o.L;
  T xx = 0, mm = 0;
  for (int k = 0; k < L * o.nch; k++) { xx += x[k] * x[k]; mm += m[k] * m[k]; }
  T den = t_sqrt(xx) * t_sqrt(mm);
  if (den <= 0) { *best_lag = 0; return T(1); }
  T best = -2; int lag = 0;
  for (int w = -o.maxshift; w <= o.maxshift; w++) {
    T cc = 0;
    for (int ch = 0; ch < o.nch; ch++)
      for (int i = 0; i < L; i++) { int ix = i - w; if (ix >= 0 && ix < L) cc += x[ch * L + ix] * m[ch * L + i]; }
    cc /= den;
    if (cc > best) { best = cc; lag = w; }
  }
  *best_lag = lag;
  return T(1) - best;
}

template <typename T>
void sbd_shift(const T* x, const Opts& o, int lag, T* xw) {   // xw[i] = x[i - lag], zero outside
  const int L = o.L;
  for (int ch = 0; ch < o.nch; ch++)
    for (int i = 0; i < L; i++) { int ix = i - lag; xw[ch * L + i] = (ix >= 0 && ix < L) ? x[ch * L + ix] : T(0); }
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- one distance, any mode
template <typename T>
T distance_of(const T* x, const T* m, const Opts& o, std::vector<T>& scratch, int* lag) {
  switch (o.mode) {
    case DTW:     return dtw_table(x, m, o, scratch);
    case SOFTDTW: return softdtw_table(x, m, o, scratch);
    case SBD:     return sbd_dist(x, m, o, lag);
    default:      return pointwise(x, m, o.L * o.nch, o);
  }
}

// the item as the update sees it from prototype m: warped, shifted, or itself
template <typename T>
void item_for(const T* x, const T* m, const Opts& o, std::vector<T>& scratch, int lag, T* xw) {
  const int D = o.L * o.nch;
  switch (o.mode) {
    case DTW:     dtw_table(x, m, o, scratch); dtw_warp(x, o, scratch, xw); break;
    case SOFTDTW: softdtw_table(x, m, o, scratch); softdtw_warp(x, m, o, scratch, xw); break;
    case SBD:     sbd_shift(x, o, lag, xw); break;
    default:      for (int k = 0; k < D; k++) xw[k] = x[k];
  }
}

static Opts make_opts(int mode, int L, int nch, int band, double p, double gamma, int maxshift, bool kahan) {
  Opts o; o.mode = mode; o.L = L; o.nch = nch; o.band = band < 0 ? L : band; o.p = p; o.gamma = gamma;
  o.maxshift = maxshift < 0 ? L - 1 : maxshift; o.kahan = kahan;
  return o;
}

// -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- the training loop
template <typename T>
List train_T(const NumericMatrix& X, const NumericMatrix& M0, const NumericMatrix& grid_dist,
             const IntegerVector& pick, const NumericVector& alpha, const NumericVector& radius,
             const NumericVector& temp, const Opts& o, double conscience, double huber, double momentum,
             const IntegerVector& snap_at) {
  const int N = X.nrow(), D = X.ncol(), K = M0.nrow(), S = pick.size();
  std::vector<T> Xt((size_t) N * D), M((size_t) K * D), V, G((size_t) K * K);
  for (int n = 0; n < N; n++) for (int d = 0; d < D; d++) Xt[(size_t) n * D + d] = T(X(n, d));
  for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) for (int d = 0; d < D; d++) M[(size_t) k * D + d] = T(M0(k, d));
  for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) for (int j = 0; j < K; j++) G[(size_t) k * K + j] = T(grid_dist(k, j));
  if (momentum > 0) V.assign((size_t) K * D, T(0));
  std::vector<T> d(K), h((size_t) K * K), w(K), P(K), e(K), xw(D), scratch, pfreq(K, T(1) / T(K));
  std::vector<int> lag(K, 0), win(S), nearest(S), counts(K, 0);
  std::vector<int> snaps(snap_at.begin(), snap_at.end());
  std::vector<double> gap(S);                                    // (d_2nd - d_1st) / d_1st: how close the contest was
  List snapshots;
  long comparisons = 0;
  T last_r = -1;
  const T mu = T(momentum), hub = T(huber), beta = T(conscience);
  for (int s = 0; s < S; s++) {
    const T* x = &Xt[(size_t) (pick[s] - 1) * D];
    const T a = T(alpha[s]), r = T(radius[s]), tmp = T(temp[s]);
    if (r != last_r) {                                           // the neighbourhood matrix, once per radius value
      for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) for (int j = 0; j < K; j++) {
        T g = G[(size_t) k * K + j];
        h[(size_t) k * K + j] = t_exp(-g * g / (T(2) * r * r));
      }
      last_r = r;
    }
    // 1. distances to every prototype
    int near = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) {
      d[k] = distance_of(x, &M[(size_t) k * D], o, scratch, &lag[k]);
      if (d[k] < d[near]) near = k;
    }
    comparisons += K;
    nearest[s] = near + 1;
    {
      T second = big<T>();
      for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) if (k != near && d[k] < second) second = d[k];
      T dn = d[near];
      gap[s] = (K > 1 && second < big<T>() / 2) ? (double) ((second - dn) / (dn > 0 ? dn : T(1))) : NA_REAL;
    }
    // 2. the winner, or the soft assignment
    int winner = near;
    if (beta > 0) {
      T best = d[0] * (T(1) + beta * (T(K) * pfreq[0] - T(1)));
      winner = 0;
      for (int k = 1; k < K; k++) {
        T v = d[k] * (T(1) + beta * (T(K) * pfreq[k] - T(1)));
        if (v < best) { best = v; winner = k; }
      }
      for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) pfreq[k] += T(0.0001) * ((k == winner ? T(1) : T(0)) - pfreq[k]);
    }
    if (tmp > 0) {                                               // deterministic annealing: a softmax over the units
      T emin = big<T>();
      for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) {
        T ek = 0;
        for (int j = 0; j < K; j++) ek += h[(size_t) k * K + j] * d[j] * d[j];
        e[k] = ek;
        if (ek < emin) emin = ek;
      }
      T Z = 0;
      for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) { P[k] = t_exp(-(e[k] - emin) / tmp); Z += P[k]; }
      int argmax = 0;
      for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) { P[k] /= Z; if (P[k] > P[argmax]) argmax = k; }
      winner = argmax;                                           // reported winner: the most probable unit
      for (int j = 0; j < K; j++) { T wj = 0; for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) wj += P[k] * h[(size_t) k * K + j]; w[j] = wj; }
    } else {
      for (int j = 0; j < K; j++) w[j] = h[(size_t) winner * K + j];
    }
    win[s] = winner + 1;
    counts[winner]++;
    // 3. the update of every unit the item pulls
    for (int j = 0; j < K; j++) {
      if (w[j] <= T(1e-10)) continue;
      T* m = &M[(size_t) j * D];
      item_for(x, m, o, scratch, lag[j], xw.data());
      T step = a * w[j];
      for (int k = 0; k < D; k++) {
        T delta = xw[k] - m[k];
        if (hub > 0) { if (delta > hub) delta = hub; else if (delta < -hub) delta = -hub; }
        if (mu > 0) { T* v = &V[(size_t) j * D + k]; *v = mu * *v + step * delta; m[k] += *v; }
        else m[k] += step * delta;
      }
    }
    if (!snaps.empty() && std::find(snaps.begin(), snaps.end(), s + 1) != snaps.end()) {
      NumericMatrix Ms(K, D);
      for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) for (int dd = 0; dd < D; dd++) Ms(k, dd) = (double) M[(size_t) k * D + dd];
      snapshots.push_back(Ms);
    }
  }
  NumericMatrix Mout(K, D);
  for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) for (int dd = 0; dd < D; dd++) Mout(k, dd) = (double) M[(size_t) k * D + dd];
  return List::create(_["M"] = Mout, _["win"] = IntegerVector(win.begin(), win.end()),
                      _["nearest"] = IntegerVector(nearest.begin(), nearest.end()),
                      _["counts"] = IntegerVector(counts.begin(), counts.end()),
                      _["gap"] = NumericVector(gap.begin(), gap.end()),
                      _["comparisons"] = (double) comparisons, _["snapshots"] = snapshots);
}

// [[Rcpp::export]]
List som_train_cpp(NumericMatrix X, NumericMatrix M0, NumericMatrix grid_dist, IntegerVector pick,
                   NumericVector alpha, NumericVector radius, NumericVector temp,
                   int mode, int L, int nch, int band, double p, double gamma, int maxshift,
                   double conscience, double huber, double momentum, int prec, bool kahan,
                   IntegerVector snap_at) {
  if (X.ncol() != L * nch) stop("X has %d columns but L * nch = %d", X.ncol(), L * nch);
  if (pick.size() != alpha.size() || pick.size() != radius.size() || pick.size() != temp.size())
    stop("pick, alpha, radius and temp must have one value per step");
  Opts o = make_opts(mode, L, nch, band, p, gamma, maxshift, kahan);
  switch (prec) {
    case P_FLOAT:      return train_T<float>(X, M0, grid_dist, pick, alpha, radius, temp, o, conscience, huber, momentum, snap_at);
    case P_LONGDOUBLE: return train_T<long double>(X, M0, grid_dist, pick, alpha, radius, temp, o, conscience, huber, momentum, snap_at);
    case P_QUAD:       return train_T<__float128>(X, M0, grid_dist, pick, alpha, radius, temp, o, conscience, huber, momentum, snap_at);
    default:           return train_T<double>(X, M0, grid_dist, pick, alpha, radius, temp, o, conscience, huber, momentum, snap_at);
  }
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- distances for judging
// every item of X against every row of M, in double: the table from which the winners and the measures come
// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericMatrix cross_dist_cpp(NumericMatrix X, NumericMatrix M, int mode, int L, int nch, int band,
                             double p, double gamma, int maxshift) {
  const int N = X.nrow(), K = M.nrow(), D = X.ncol();
  if (D != L * nch || M.ncol() != D) stop("X and M must have L * nch columns");
  Opts o = make_opts(mode, L, nch, band, p, gamma, maxshift, false);
  std::vector<double> x(D), m((size_t) K * D), scratch;
  for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) for (int d = 0; d < D; d++) m[(size_t) k * D + d] = M(k, d);
  NumericMatrix out(N, K);
  int lag;
  for (int n = 0; n < N; n++) {
    for (int d = 0; d < D; d++) x[d] = X(n, d);
    for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) out(n, k) = distance_of(x.data(), &m[(size_t) k * D], o, scratch, &lag);
  }
  return out;
}

// the item warped, shifted or copied as the update of prototype m would see it (for pictures and checks)
// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericVector item_seen_cpp(NumericVector x, NumericVector m, int mode, int L, int nch, int band,
                            double p, double gamma, int maxshift) {
  Opts o = make_opts(mode, L, nch, band, p, gamma, maxshift, false);
  std::vector<double> xx(x.begin(), x.end()), mm(m.begin(), m.end()), scratch, xw(x.size());
  int lag = 0;
  distance_of(xx.data(), mm.data(), o, scratch, &lag);
  item_for(xx.data(), mm.data(), o, scratch, lag, xw.data());
  return NumericVector(xw.begin(), xw.end());
}

// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- topographic product
// Bauer & Pawelzik (1992): P = 1 / (K (K - 1)) sum_j sum_k log P3(j, k). dV: distances between prototypes
// in the data space; dA: distances on the map. Ties on the map are broken by the data distance.
// [[Rcpp::export]]
double topographic_product_cpp(NumericMatrix dV, NumericMatrix dA) {
  const int K = dV.nrow();
  if (K < 3) return 0;
  double total = 0;
  std::vector<int> nV(K - 1), nA(K - 1), idx(K - 1);
  for (int j = 0; j < K; j++) {
    int c = 0;
    for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) if (k != j) idx[c++] = k;
    std::vector<int> oV = idx, oA = idx;
    std::sort(oV.begin(), oV.end(), [&](int a, int b) {
      if (dV(j, a) != dV(j, b)) return dV(j, a) < dV(j, b);
      if (dA(j, a) != dA(j, b)) return dA(j, a) < dA(j, b);
      return a < b; });
    std::sort(oA.begin(), oA.end(), [&](int a, int b) {
      if (dA(j, a) != dA(j, b)) return dA(j, a) < dA(j, b);
      if (dV(j, a) != dV(j, b)) return dV(j, a) < dV(j, b);
      return a < b; });
    double logprod = 0;
    for (int k = 1; k <= K - 1; k++) {
      double q1 = dV(j, oA[k - 1]) / dV(j, oV[k - 1]);
      double q2 = dA(j, oA[k - 1]) / dA(j, oV[k - 1]);
      if (!(q1 > 0) || !(q2 > 0) || !std::isfinite(q1) || !std::isfinite(q2)) { q1 = q2 = 1; }
      logprod += std::log(q1) + std::log(q2);
      total += logprod / (2.0 * k);
    }
  }
  return total / ((double) K * (K - 1));
}

// shortest ways along the map between all units, each step as long as the distance between the two
// prototypes (for the Kaski-Lagus error); 'links' is 1 where two units are direct neighbours
// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericMatrix map_ways_cpp(NumericMatrix dV, IntegerMatrix links) {
  const int K = dV.nrow();
  const double INF = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
  NumericMatrix P(K, K);
  for (int a = 0; a < K; a++) for (int b = 0; b < K; b++) P(a, b) = (a == b) ? 0 : (links(a, b) ? dV(a, b) : INF);
  for (int k = 0; k < K; k++) for (int a = 0; a < K; a++) {
    double pak = P(a, k);
    if (pak == INF) continue;
    for (int b = 0; b < K; b++) { double v = pak + P(k, b); if (v < P(a, b)) P(a, b) = v; }
  }
  return P;
}
```
